node.label: Veronica Strong-Boag
node.date_label: The Parliament of Women (1976) · Rethinking Canada (1986) · The New Day Recalled (1988) · Contested Space (1994)
node.description: In The New Day Recalled (1988), Strong-Boag argues that class differences did not displace the gender hierarchy shaping girls’ and women’s lives in interwar English Canada. Its modified life-course approach connects paid work, household labour, family and ageing. Patricia Rooke praised the research but criticized its empiricism and underdeveloped theoretical explanations. Strong-Boag’s co-edited Rethinking Canada began in 1986 with Anita Clair Fellman; the fourth edition (2002) was edited with Mona Gleason and Adele Perry. In her presidential address “Contested Space” (1994), she argued that historians must confront their own privilege and connect political history with the experiences of people excluded from national narratives. Her review of J. L. Granatstein (1999) defended inclusive national history while agreeing that history teaching needed support. Later books examined adoption and disadvantaged childhoods through intersecting inequalities.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Parliament of Women (1976); Rethinking Canada: The Promise of Women’s History (1986, co-edited with Anita Clair Fellman; fourth edition 2002, with Mona Gleason and Adele Perry); The New Day Recalled (1988); “Contested Space” (1994); Paddling Her Own Canoe (2000, with Carole Gerson); Finding Families, Finding Ourselves (2006); Fostering Nation? (2011).
node.scope_note: The New Day Recalled is known through Rooke’s complete review; the monographs and Rethinking Canada editions were not read in full. Selected primary passages of the 1994 address, the complete 1999 review, selected Sangster reprint passages, institutional bibliographies and the 2023 questionnaire were read. The 1992 co-authored reply and the 1996 labour-history exchange remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Strong-Boag and Joan Sangster co-authored “Teaching Canadian History in the 1990s: Whose National History Are We Lamenting?” (1992), with Linda Kealey and Ruth Roach Pierson.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Strong-Boag’s institutional CV, non-refereed journals section (UBC embedded CV; also UVic PDF p. 12), lists all four authors and JCS 27:2, 129–131. Bibliographic collaboration only: original article body inaccessible; no individual allocation of its argument. Existing source cdng_l_kealey_et_al_1992 is reused without upgrading its original metadata-only verification.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 1999 review of Granatstein’s Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), Strong-Boag rejects its marginalization of women, workers and racialized people while agreeing that Canadian history needs stronger teaching.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete review, pp. 283–285, read in the Queen’s journal PDF (1625/1713), ending at Strong-Boag’s signature on 285 before the next review. Especially 284: reforms require “faithful accounts of the past”; she supports some teaching proposals but contests the book’s hierarchy of significance. Granatstein’s book unread. The older graph source’s unread-review note is preserved, with a separate fresh-read addendum proposed.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Contested Space” (1994), Strong-Boag criticizes Creighton’s dismissal of radical historical reinterpretations and his opposition to cultural pluralism, citing his 1969 essay and Canada’s First Century (1970).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected official Érudit PDF passages, printed p. 7, nn. 15–16: she calls his position “blinkered vision”; n. 15 identifies “John A. Macdonald, Confederation and the Canadian West” in Minorities Schools and Politics (1969), p. 9, and n. 16 identifies Canada’s First Century, 106–109. This is her attributed criticism; Creighton originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Strong-Boag, with Jean Barman, supervised Adele Perry’s postdoctoral fellowship in 1998–99. Strong-Boag and Perry later co-edited the fourth edition of Rethinking Canada: The Promise of Women’s History (2002), with Mona Gleason.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Strong-Boag’s institutional CV, PDF leaf 34, heading “Post-doctoral supervision,” which lists Perry (York), SSHRCC, 1998–9, with Jean Barman. PDF leaf 4 lists the three editors of Rethinking Canada, fourth edition (2002). Supervision supplies the directed influence classification; the co-editing is a separate undirected collaboration retained as a second witness. No particular theoretical debt or sole supervision is claimed. Fold into the existing pair rather than adding a duplicate edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: Strong-Boag, Jean Barman and Neil Sutherland jointly compiled A Bibliography of Canadian Childhood: Articles (1987).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Strong-Boag’s UBC embedded CV, Non-refereed publications / Other, explicitly credits the 1987 bibliography to herself with Sutherland and Barman. This is a bibliographical collaboration only; no claim of common theoretical commitments or reading of the bibliography itself. The same credit is in the UVic CV, PDF p. 15.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Contested Space” (1994), Strong-Boag uses Dubinsky’s Improper Advances (1993) to connect the historical disbelief of sexual-assault complainants with the exclusions of Canadian collective memory.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected primary PDF, printed p. 16, n. 64: Strong-Boag quotes Dubinsky’s conclusion about complainants leaving the “courtroom empty-handed” and extends that pattern to collective responses to abuse. Printed p. 5 n. 5 also draws on Dubinsky’s 1993 labour-history teaching essay. Only the first substantive use is proposed; Dubinsky’s book unread. No complainant’s words or narrative are reproduced.

proposed_edges.relationship: The New Day Recalled (1988) uses a modified life-course approach to show how gender hierarchy persisted across class differences in interwar English Canada.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated by Rooke’s 1989 review, pp. 165–166: outlines six life-course chapters and quotes the book’s p. 3 on class not superseding sex stratification. Book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reflecting on Finding Families, Finding Ourselves (2006) and Fostering Nation? (2011) in her 2023 CHA questionnaire, Strong-Boag presents disadvantaged childhoods as inseparable from inequalities of gender, class, race, sexuality and disability.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: CHA questionnaire, answer to “of all your writings, which are you most proud of and why?” She describes both books in these terms; the claim is her retrospective account, not a fresh reading of either monograph. Original years checked in the CV, PDF p. 3.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Contested Space” (1994) counters laments for a single national history by arguing that historical accounts must connect political institutions with the histories of women, workers and racialized people.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected primary PDF, printed pp. 4–6 and 17: her alternative requires “many interwoven narratives” (6). This intervention precedes Who Killed Canadian History? (1998); it is not described as a reply to that book. The existing field-to-debate edge_813 is preserved; this is a person-level route supported by newly read primary passages.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Contested Space: The Politics of Canadian Memory” (1994) argues that collective memory becomes more adequate when historians confront professional privilege and include histories of violence and exclusion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected primary PDF, printed pp. 14–17, especially concluding p. 17: “meaningful memory for all Canadians”. Claim concerns the scholarly programme, without reproducing survivors’ accounts. Other parts of the address were sampled, not a complete fresh reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her historiographical essay 'By Necessity or by Right' (2002), Nancy Christie discusses Strong-Boag's 'The Girl of the New Day' (1979) as characterising women's work in the 1920s as gendered continuity rather than new job segregation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Body-text engagement read on pp. 121–123. Christie uses Strong-Boag’s findings in her historiographical explanation; this supports specific uptake, not supervision or a general intellectual genealogy.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Rethinking Canada (1986), co-edited by Strong-Boag and Anita Clair Fellman, in 1987, Bettina Bradbury judged that it showed Canadian women's history becoming more sophisticated, and suggested that future collections focus on specific themes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete journal review read, pp. 454–455. The closing recommendation mildly qualifies a positive appraisal; it concerns the collection’s format rather than rejecting Strong-Boag’s McClung argument. The journal credits its French translation to John A. Dickinson.

proposed_edges.relationship: Strong-Boag’s ‘The Girl of the New Day’ (1979) contributed to labour history by explaining persistent gender hierarchies within industrial modernization, as Nancy Christie discusses in 2002.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Christie substantively credits Strong-Boag alongside Sangster and McCallum. The contribution is shared, not a claim of sole innovation; the individual uptake is separately represented by o_01.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Last Suffragist Standing (2018), Strong-Boag contributed to biographical method through a contextual account of Laura Marshall Jamieson that analyzes gender, race, class and privilege, as Kesia Kvill’s 2019 review explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete review read, pp. 352–354. Kvill identifies a method for writing about a woman who left few sources, while criticizing the contextual approach for sometimes displacing Jamieson and understating personal experience. This is review-based evidence; the book was not read. Kvill lacks an eligible person endpoint, so no reviewer edge is proposed.
